verses.translation_literal: A psalm, of David, in his being in the wilderness of Judah.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David, from the days when he was in the wilderness of Judah.
verses.directors_commentary: In the Hebrew Bible this heading is verse 1 and counts as part of the psalm; the KJV prints it unnumbered, which is why every verse of this psalm in your English Bible sits one lower than here. It places the psalm in the open country of Judah, east and south of Jerusalem, a hill land that falls away into the Dead Sea basin and gets almost no rain. The traditions attach it to David as a fugitive from Saul (Rashi on Psalm 63:1 cites 1 Samuel 22–24; Radak says he was fleeing from Saul), so the actor should hear the voice of a man who has been hunted into a place with no cover and no water. The KJV's 'when he was' is fine, but the Hebrew has a verbal noun, 'in his being', which gives the line a sense of a state he is still in rather than a past event. Note also that 'wilderness' (midbar) here is steppe and badlands, not sand dunes: it supports sheep in the spring and nothing in summer.

philological_notes.note: A psalm: a song sung to an instrument, from the root meaning 'to make music, to pluck'. It marks the text as a performed piece, not a private prayer.
The wilderness of Judah. Radak identifies it as the wilderness of Ziph, which is where David hid from Saul (Radak on Psalm 63:1); Rashi cites 1 Samuel 22–24.

verses.translation_literal: God, my God [are] you; I seek you [at dawn]: thirsted for you has my soul, pined for you has my flesh, in a land of dryness and weary, without water.
verses.translation_dramatic: God. You are my God, and I come looking for you with the first grey of the morning. My whole self is thirsting for you. My very body aches with wanting you, here in this dry and weary land where there is no water at all.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with a name and a claim in one breath: 'God — my God are you.' Speak it as something said out loud in an empty place, the first words of a man whose only audience is the sky. The verb 'ashachareka' is probably from shachar, 'dawn', so 'I seek you at dawn'; the KJV's 'early will I seek thee' keeps this, though it makes it a future promise and drops the immediacy. It may also be from another root meaning 'seek'; Ibn Ezra offers both, and Rashi compares Job 8:5, 'if you seek God.' The 'soul' (nefesh) is literally the throat, the gullet that goes dry; the line asks you to feel thirst in the body, not a mood. The word 'kamah' ('pined') occurs only here in the Bible; Radak and Ibn Ezra both say it has no parallel, which is why every English version guesses at 'longeth'. The KJV also softens 'weary' to 'thirsty' in the last line, which hides that the Hebrew describes the land itself as worn out, not just dry: a place that exhausts the traveller. In the climate of Judah the dry season runs from May to October, with no rain at all and wadis (seasonal streambeds) that stay empty; a man without water there can last perhaps two or three days.

philological_notes.note: 'I seek you', most likely from shachar 'dawn' ('I seek you at first light'), though it may also be from a root meaning 'seek eagerly' as in Proverbs 11:27. Rashi explains it as 'seek and search', citing Job 7:21 and 8:5; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to the 'shocher tov' of Proverbs 11.
'Pined, longed'; a unique word in the Bible. Rashi says it means desire and has no parallel; Radak and Metzudat Zion say the same.
A dry, parched land; the word is used for desert and for places with no water at all. Rashi glosses it 'in the wilderness'.

verses.translation_literal: So in the sanctuary I have seen you, to see your strength and your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I have looked on you in the holy place, and that is why I long to see your strength again, and your glory.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse starts with 'ken', 'so, thus': this is the hinge of the psalm. It links the thirst of verse 2 to a memory. Because he once saw God in the holy place, he now thirsts. The KJV turns the sentence around ('To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary'), which blurs the claim and makes it sound like a comparison. The Hebrew says first, plainly, 'In the sanctuary I have seen you.' Rashi reads 'ken' as 'ka'asher' (as): 'I thirst to see your strength and glory as I saw you in the Shiloh sanctuary.' 'Strength' ('oz) and 'glory' (kavod) are, in the tradition of Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David, the Ark and the Presence resting on it; Metzudat Zion cites 'the ark of your strength' (Psalm 132:8). Malbim takes 'seen' as a vision of the mind, and the wish to see as the longing to see with the eyes of the body. Either way the actor should play a man who remembers a place and an experience, not an abstract idea of holiness: the worship space was where the public could see God's rule in action.

philological_notes.note: 'I have seen you', from chazah, a verb for visionary seeing, used of prophets. The psalmist's second verb, lir'ot 'to see', uses the ordinary word; the pair 'seen / to see' is a play on two kinds of sight. Malbim distinguishes the two as seeing with the mind and seeing with the eye.
'Your strength'. The tradition reads it as the Ark, the visible sign of God's power (Radak on Psalms 63:3 and Metzudat Zion, citing Psalm 132:8).

verses.translation_literal: For good [is] your loyal love, more than lives; my lips will extol you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Better than life itself is your faithful love. It is better than breath, better than every year I have been given. And so my lips will not keep silent; they will lift up your praise.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the speaker weighs two things and declares that one outweighs the other. Chesed is not mere kindness: in the Near Eastern world it is the loyalty a stronger party owes a weaker one under a bond, the faithful love that keeps a covenant when it would be easier to break it. For a man hiding in the wilderness, with his life in daily danger, to say that this is better than life is a daring claim, and the actors should not rush it. The Hebrew says 'than lives', a plural, and the plural is the point: not this one fragile life but life in every form. The KJV's 'lovingkindness' is Coverdale's coinage, a lovely word, but it softens a term of law and loyalty into a sentiment, and it turns the Hebrew's plain 'good' into the comparative 'better' without noting that the verse simply says 'good is your chesed, from lives'. The verb 'extol' (shabach) is a stronger and rarer word than the 'praise' the KJV uses; it is to speak up and magnify aloud. Malbim hears the verse as an argument: life is only the means by which the lips can praise, so the loyal love that gives the reason is better than the means. Metzudat David hears it more simply: without praise, what are the days for.

philological_notes.note: Loyal love, covenant faithfulness, the loyalty that keeps a bond. I gloss it 'covenant loyalty' as my own reading; English 'kindness' or 'lovingkindness' loses the sense of obligation. Metzudat David and Malbim both understand it here as the gift of life itself, and as better than that gift.

'From lives', in a plural of intensity and extent, with min as the comparative 'more than'. The KJV flattens it into the singular 'life'. Malbim argues that life is only the means to praise, which is why chesed outranks it.

verses.translation_literal: Thus I will bless you in my life; in your name I will lift up my palms.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I will bless you for as long as I live. I will stand and lift my open hands, and I will do it in your name.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'thus' (ken) looks back: because your loyal love is good, therefore this. Rashi reads it as 'then', the way the Targum renders it elsewhere, so that the blessing follows the arrival before God. The gesture is the key to the scene. Lifting the palms (kappayim, the open hands, not the closed fists the KJV's 'hands' might suggest) is the ancient posture of prayer and of oath: the open, empty hand held up to heaven that says, I come with nothing, and I wait to be given. Rashi says the lifting is 'to pray and to praise'; Radak, more soldier than saint, hears in it the help of God to find strength for his hands against those who fight him, a reminder that the same palms that rise in prayer are the palms that wage war. The KJV's 'while I live' is fair but turns a phrase, 'in my lives', into a time clause; the Hebrew says literally 'in my life', and Malbim presses the point: he will not bless God for the life itself, but for the loyal love that lets him praise. The Targum pushes the whole verse towards the world to come, which the Hebrew does not say.

philological_notes.note: 'I will lift up my palms', the posture of prayer. Rashi glosses it 'to pray and to praise'; Radak instead takes it as the strength of the hands that fight enemies, in God's name.

verses.translation_literal: As [with] fat and fatness my soul will be sated, and [with] lips of cries of joy my mouth will praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul will be filled as a man is filled at a feast, with the richest portion, rich and running with fat. And my mouth will sing, and my lips will ring with joy.
verses.directors_commentary: The image is a feast, and the actor should taste it. Chelev (the fat) and deshen (the fatness) are the best cuts of the sacrificial animal, the portions set aside for God and for honored guests, and in a land where meat was rare, where most people ate bread and lentils and a lamb meant a holiday, to be 'sated' with them is to be as well-fed as a man can imagine. The speaker is in the wilderness, hungry, and the soul he has been starving (see 'my soul thirsts' in verse 2, the one word that returns here) is fed not on meat but on praise. The KJV's 'marrow and fatness' invents the marrow: the Hebrew has fat, and the YLT's 'milk' mistakes the word for a similar one. 'Soul' is nefesh, the throat and appetite as well as the self, and the sating has two directions: the soul is sated and the mouth sings. Metzudat David and Malbim hear the sating as the result of the praise itself. Radak reads the 'and' in 'and lips' as 'when': when my lips of joy praise, it is sweet to me, as fat is sweet to a hungry man. Rashi reads 'lips' as 'tongues', languages, with a proof from 'one lip' in Genesis 11:1.

philological_notes.note: 'Fat and fatness', a doubling of the same idea in two words (Radak: a repetition of meaning in different words). Chelev is the choice, best part, as in Genesis 45:18, which Metzudat Zion cites; the KJV's 'marrow' is not in the Hebrew.
'Lips of cries of joy'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read 'lips' as 'speech' or 'languages' (as in 'one lip', Genesis 11:1); Metzudat David has 'many tongues of rejoicing'.

verses.translation_literal: If I have remembered you upon my beds, in the night-watches I murmur on you.
verses.translation_dramatic: When I lie down and think of you, when sleep will not come and the night is long, I turn your name over in the dark, I whisper it over and over, through every watch of the night.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene is night, and the actor should make it quiet. The Hebrew 'im' is usually 'if', and the KJV's 'when' makes a condition into a habit. Radak and Ibn Ezra defend that: 'im' can stand where 'when' would, so that the verse describes what he does as often as the night comes. Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it instead as 'truly': truly I remember you on my bed. Both readings are good, and the second makes the line a statement of fact rather than a condition. 'Beds' is a plural (yetzu'ai), and Radak notes why: he did not sleep in one place but in many, fleeing from place to place, so these are not the beds of a household but the hard places of a fugitive. The night was kept in three watches, and Radak and Metzudat Zion say these are the three times a man wakes from sleep. 'Meditate' (hagah) is far closer to murmuring: the word is used of a lion growling over prey and of a dove's low cooing. It is the sound a man makes as he mutters to himself, and the KJV's polite 'meditate' loses it. The Targum adds 'by your word', a note of its own.

philological_notes.note: Usually 'if'. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as 'when, whenever'; Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it as 'truly'. The literal layer keeps 'if' so that both readings remain open.
The night-watches, the three parts into which the night was divided, and the times a man wakes from sleep.
To mutter, murmur, or meditate aloud. Rashi glosses it 'I think on you'. The sense of low sound is my own reading of the root.

verses.translation_literal: For you have been a help for me, and in the shadow of your wings I will cry for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you have been my help. You were there when no one else was. And so, under the shadow of your wings, I will cry out for joy.
verses.directors_commentary: 'For' gives the reason for the praise: he has been helped. The Hebrew 'ezrah' is a help, a noun, and the ending is a little more than needed, so the sense is 'you have become a help to me' rather than simply 'my help' as the KJV has it. Radak says this was the case against all who pursued him: they did not catch him or do him harm. 'The shadow of your wings' is a picture of a bird sheltering its young, and also, in the Near East, of the winged guardian figures, the sun-disc with spread wings, that stood over kings and temple doors; to say it of the LORD is to claim the protection of the greatest of patrons. The KJV's 'therefore' is not in the Hebrew: the verse says 'and', and the joy is a second thing, not a consequence. The word for rejoicing, ranan, is the one for a ringing cry, and the KJV's 'rejoice' is milder than the shout. The Targum has 'in the shadow of your Shekhinah', replacing the bird with the divine presence.

philological_notes.note: 'Your wings', the image of a bird shielding its young. The Targum renders it 'your Shekhinah', God's dwelling presence, to avoid the bodily image.

verses.translation_literal: My soul has clung after you; on me your right [hand] has held.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul clings to you and will not let go, and your right hand holds me up.
verses.directors_commentary: Two verbs, two directions: his soul clings, and God's hand holds. Dabak is the verb used of a man cleaving to his wife in Genesis 2:24 and of a tongue sticking to a parched palate: something that is stuck fast. The KJV's 'followeth hard after' is a hunter's phrase and makes the soul sound as if it is in pursuit; the Hebrew has it glued, not chasing. 'After you' (acharekha) is the preposition 'behind', so the cling is that of one who walks behind. The second half answers the first: 'your right hand' is the hand of strength, and 'upholdeth' is the verb 'to grasp and support'. Rashi says the support is 'that I should not fall'; Radak and Metzudat David say that the cling gives him the right to be supported, so that he does not fall to his pursuers and does not totter. Ibn Ezra goes further: God's hand is what enabled him to cling at all. The Targum has the soul cling 'after your Torah'.

philological_notes.note: To cleave, stick, cling, the verb of a bond that cannot be loosed. The KJV 'followeth hard after' turns it into pursuit.
'Your right hand has held'. Rashi: 'that I should not fall'. Ibn Ezra: God's hand also helped him to cling.

verses.translation_literal: And they, to ruin they seek my soul; they will go into the lowest parts of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: But those who hunt my life for its ruin will go down themselves, down into the lowest places of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns on a single word, 'and they' (vehemah), a pronoun pointed at the enemies like a finger, and Rashi and Radak simply say: my enemies, the ones who chase me. The Hebrew 'to ruin' (lesho'ah) is a noun, not the KJV's verb 'to destroy it': they seek my soul for ruin, to make a desolation of it, as Radak puts it, and Metzudat Zion defines the word as 'desolation'. The 'soul' is again nefesh, the life and breath; to seek someone's nefesh is the idiom for hunting them to death. Then the reversal: they will go into 'the lowest parts of the earth', the underworld. Rashi says it is a low place, Sheol and the pit, where they will go and fall; Radak says the line is a prayer, not a prophecy. Metzudat David and Meiri identify the pursuers as Saul and his men. Malbim has a different reading: the lowest parts are the caves and holes in the wilderness where they searched for David. Rashi also hears an ambush in the verse, an attack on a day of darkness when he would not notice them. The Targum has them seek him 'for burial', turning ruin into the grave. The KJV's 'shall go' hides the possible wish in 'will go'.

philological_notes.note: 'To ruin, desolation'. Radak understands it as making his life a ruin, and Metzudat Zion glosses it as desolation. A noun, which the KJV's verb 'to destroy it' turns into an action.
'The lowest parts of the earth'. Rashi and Radak: Sheol, the pit. Malbim: the caves and holes of the wilderness where David was hunted.

verses.translation_literal: They will pour him over the hands of the sword; a portion of foxes they will be.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will be poured out to the sword, and left on the field, and the foxes will have them for their share.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the harshest line of the psalm, and it should not be softened. 'Yagiruhu' is from a verb meaning to pour or flow, and it is used of water running and of blood spilled: they will be 'poured out' over 'the hands of the sword', the idiom for the power of the blade. The KJV's 'they shall fall' hides this picture, and the ASV's 'given over to the power of the sword' keeps only half. Metzudat Zion cites the pouring of water; Metzudat David, those who pour out blood by the sword; Rashi hears dragging, as water drags a bank away; Radak and Meiri say it is blood running from the dead. The verb is plural and the object singular, 'they will pour him', and Radak takes the singular as Saul, the others as his men. Rashi adds that the text is short and does not say who does the pouring. The second half is a vivid and common curse: the 'portion' (menat) is the share assigned at a meal or in a division of spoil, and here the share is the dead's body, a meal for foxes. In the ancient world, to lie unburied for scavengers was the worst of ends, since it cut a man off from his family tomb. Radak says the foxes and wild beasts eat the corpses. Rashi compares Lamentations 5:18, where foxes walk on a ruined Zion. Meiri notes that the blood stands in for the whole body. The KJV's 'foxes' is correct.

philological_notes.note: From the verb for pouring or flowing. Rashi reads it as dragging, like water pulling, and Metzudat Zion as pouring and spilling, as in water that runs. Radak connects it to blood running from the sword. Plural verb, singular object.
'A portion for foxes', the share set aside for scavengers. Radak: they will be slain and the foxes and wild animals will eat them. Rashi compares Lamentations 5:18.

verses.translation_literal: And the king will rejoice in God; he will boast, every one who swears by him, for the mouth of speakers of falsehood will be shut.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the king will rejoice in God. All who swear by his name will glory in it, while the mouths of liars are sealed shut.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends on a king, and it is the one place where the reader must decide who is speaking. Ibn Ezra reports that some say the king is Saul, but holds that it is David; Radak and Metzudat David say the speaker speaks of himself; Rashi, too, notes that David had already been anointed. The setting is the wilderness, and the title of the psalm places the author in Judah's desert; the one who 'will rejoice' is the anointed fugitive. 'Swears by him' is the other puzzle: the Hebrew has only 'him' (bo), which may be God or the king. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take it as God, those who cleave to God and swear by his name; Meiri and Malbim allow that the king is meant, since men swore by the king's life, as in 'as Pharaoh lives'. An oath in the ancient world called down a god as witness and punishment, so it is the mark of loyalty: only the honest can swear and not fear. The final image is of 'shutting' the mouth, from sakar, to stop up, the word used of the springs of the deep being stopped in Genesis 8:2, as Rashi and Metzudat Zion note. The KJV's 'stopped' keeps that, though 'boast' for yithalel is a good deal harder than the KJV's 'glory'. The speakers of 'falsehood' (sheker) are the slanderers, a figure that shifts the contest from swords to words.

philological_notes.note: 'The one who swears by him'. Antecedent disputed: God (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David) or the king (Meiri, Malbim's second option, Ibn Ezra's report of 'some'). The Hebrew has only 'him'.
'It will be shut up, stopped'. Rashi glosses it 'will be sealed' and compares the springs of the deep, Genesis 8:2; Metzudat Zion defines it as 'shut'.
